intro: Read the deck for the facts and these notes for the thinking. Each note explains a slide, gives you something to remember or warns where people slip. Work the examples in pencil, answer the recall questions before you check, and add your own marks beside mine.

sections.title: What Community Development Is
sections.big_idea: Community development builds a community's **capacity to act**, and the test is whether it is more able to act after the project ends.
in_plain_words: Community development is a process in which people who share a place or condition act together to shape the decisions that affect their lives. The road or the well matters, and the capability the community keeps afterwards matters more. Delivering a service is legitimate, and the error is calling a service project community development and expecting self-sustaining results.

The word community needs care. A village is layered by caste, class, gender, religion and faction, so there are interests and no single community interest. Place, identity and interest are three senses that overlap. Change can be endogenous or exogenous. **Never say the community wants without asking which part**, and who was in the room.

right.title: Community development
items: Success is capacity and voice built
Main risk is slow, hard to count

diagram.caption: both have a place, and they are not the same

key_terms.meaning: People acting together to identify and act on their own needs.
Driven by the community's own priorities and resources.
Introduced by an outside agency, scheme or expert.
Telling visitors what will keep resources coming.
Claims what is owed and holds the state to account.

worked_example.title: Is it community development?
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: an agency installs a handpump in a village and leaves. Another helps the village form a water committee that repairs its own pump.
steps: Apply the third diagnostic row: what is left after exit?
The first project leaves an asset, the handpump, which is an output.
The second leaves an institution, a committee that keeps acting.
Check the other clauses: who defined the problem, and who is accountable to whom?
worked_example.answer: The first is service delivery. The second is community development, provided the committee was built on purpose and not assumed to appear.

mistakes: Calling a service-delivery project community development and being surprised when nothing sustains itself.
Treating the village as one voice. It systematically registers the preferences of whoever already dominates.
Reporting exogenous work as endogenous, which brings ownership expectations without the results.

recall.q: What is the test of good practice?
recall.a: When the project ends, is the community more able to act on its own future than before?

recall.q: Name the three senses of community.
recall.a: Place, identity and interest.

recall.q: When did India launch its Community Development Programme?
What corrective do the slides give for mixed-group bias?
recall.a: Separate group discussions by gender and social group.

recall.q: Which row is the sharpest diagnostic between service delivery and development?
recall.a: What is left after exit: the asset or the institution.

sections.title: Principles & Values
sections.big_idea: Five principles, each with a **behavioural test**, tell you whether a value is practised or only performed.
in_plain_words: The five principles are participation, empowerment, self-determination, equity and sustainability. Each has a test: could the answer have changed the design, do they now hold something they did not, have you supported a priority you disagreed with, who is in the room who would not normally be, what runs without you next year. The third test is the hardest.

Working values appear in conduct: respect, humility, transparency, accountability and do no harm. A budget on the wall in the local language is among the cheapest and most consequential acts. Every principle can be performed without being practised, and the performed version produces the evidence a report requires. **A value you cannot check by watching a meeting** is not yet operational.

diagram.caption: each with a test that is real or not

key_terms.meaning: Gaining control over decisions, resources and institutions.
The right to set one's own priorities.
Giving more support where need is greater.
Consultation inside undisclosed fixed constraints.
Never leaving a community worse or more divided.

worked_example.title: Run the five tests
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: an agency's project plan has a participation section, an inclusion policy, a transparency commitment and an empowerment objective.
steps: Participation: could the answer have changed the design? If the design never moved, it fails.
Equity: was a meeting held in the Dalit hamlet, or only the policy written?
Transparency: is the budget on the wall, in the local language?
Empowerment: does someone now hold a decision they did not before?
worked_example.answer: Each commitment passes only if the practised column is true. A proposal section alone is a value performed.

mistakes: Treating a values statement as evidence. It is compatible with failing all five tests.
Funding only the community priorities that fit the agency's theme, which fails the third test.
Expecting empowerment without friction. Power is relational, so real work produces some.

recall.q: Name the five sustainability dimensions in the table.
recall.a: Social, institutional, financial, ecological and political.

recall.q: Which sustainability row defeats most community institutions?
recall.a: Financial: a group with no independent revenue ends when the grant does.

recall.q: What does Arnstein's ladder add to the word participation?
recall.a: The rung, which names who decides.

recall.q: What is the hard test of self-determination?
recall.a: Are you willing to support a community decision you disagree with?

recall.q: Why is a unanimous gram sabha resolution weak evidence?
recall.a: It shows who was present and what could be said aloud, which is no proof of agreement.

sections.title: Participation & Its Ladder
sections.big_idea: Participation is a matter of degree, and **the only question that sorts the rungs is who decides**.
in_plain_words: Sherry Arnstein's Ladder of Citizen Participation (1969) has eight rungs in three levels: manipulation and therapy are non-participation, informing, consultation and placation are tokenism, and partnership, delegated power and citizen control are citizen power. Everything below rung six leaves the decision where it was. Tokenism looks like participation and produces the evidence a donor asks for.

Hart adapted the ladder for children, with three false rungs: manipulation, decoration, tokenism. Later thinkers add that a community may choose to be only informed, and ask who chose the level and whether the space was invited or claimed. **Diagnose your own work** with the table: most projects sit lower than they claim.

diagram.caption: Arnstein's three levels, most power at the top

key_terms.meaning: Eight rungs from manipulation to citizen control.
A token seat on a committee, with no vote.
UNICEF's 1992 adaptation for children and youth.
A space the community was invited into.
A space the community created.

worked_example.title: Find the honest rung
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: three projects describe themselves as participatory.
steps: An awareness camp tells people what will happen: informing, rung 3.
A team collects feedback and decides anyway: consultation, rung 4, which is tokenism.
The SHG gets a committee seat with no vote: placation, rung 5.
Count the levels: rungs 1-2 plus rungs 3-5 plus rungs 6-8, so 2 + 3 + 3 = 8 rungs.
worked_example.answer: Rungs 3, 4 and 5, all inside the tokenism band. To move up, ask before deciding, let feedback change something, and give the seat a vote.

mistakes: Claiming rung 8 while operating at rung 4.
Counting meetings, forms and committees as power. They fit every rung.
Assuming a ladder means higher is always right. What matters is who chose the level.

recall.q: How many rungs does Arnstein's ladder have, and in how many levels?
recall.a: Eight rungs in three levels.

recall.q: Which rungs are tokenism?
recall.a: 3 to 5: informing, consultation and placation.

recall.q: What are Hart's three false rungs?
recall.a: Manipulation, decoration and tokenism.

recall.q: What question sorts the rungs fastest?
recall.a: At the end, who signs?

recall.q: What is Cornwall's useful distinction?
recall.a: Invited versus claimed spaces.

sections.title: Asset-Based Community Development
sections.big_idea: ABCD starts from what a community **already has**, then connects assets and claims entitlements.
in_plain_words: Kretzmann and McKnight (1993) flipped the usual needs assessment. Asset mapping produces an inventory of what is present, casts the community as actor and builds a case for local action. The deficit lens does quiet harm: a community told only what it lacks learns to wait. Four asset types are individuals, associations, institutions, and physical and natural resources.

Mapping is done together and publicly, and the map stays in the village. The sequence is map, connect, mobilise, add outside help last. The breakthrough is often a new connection, such as an SHG linking to the bank. Critics say ABCD lets the state off the hook, and the answer is to do both: **map assets, then claim entitlements**.

key_terms.meaning: Asset-Based Community Development.
A map of problems and gaps that makes the community a client.
A shared picture of local capacities.
An informal group such as a savings circle.
Linking assets that do not yet talk to each other.

worked_example.title: From map to action
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a hamlet's mapping finds a retired teacher, a youth club, an SHG and a school building.
steps: Map: ask about capacity in each of the four asset types, and leave need for later.
Connect: introduce the youth club and the SHG, which have no working relationship.
Mobilise: the community chooses a goal, say coaching for children.
Add: bring outside help only for real gaps, last.
worked_example.answer: The retired teacher coaches in the school building with the youth club's help, and the SHG links to the bank. Outside help fills what is still missing.

mistakes: Bringing outside resources first. It re-establishes the agency as the source.
Treating asset-based as self-financed, which can excuse the state's withdrawal.
Leaving the map with the agency. A map the agency holds is an extraction.

recall.q: Who pioneered ABCD, and in which book?
recall.a: Kretzmann and McKnight, in Building Communities from the Inside Out.

recall.q: Name the four steps of the sequence.
recall.a: Map, connect, mobilise, add.

recall.q: What is the first answer often given when a community is asked what it has?
recall.a: What it lacks.

recall.q: What does ABCD say to the critique that it lets the state off the hook?
recall.a: It does so only if you stop before claiming entitlements.

recall.q: Which asset row carries the method's sharpest claim?
recall.a: Individuals: people written off as dependants hold assets.

sections.title: Community Organising & Mobilisation
sections.big_idea: Organising builds power through leaders from within, and **mobilising spends power while organising builds it**.
in_plain_words: Community organising asks how people without power build enough of it to win change from those who have it. It names a target, the person who can grant the demand. Alinsky's tradition holds that change comes from organised people. Mobilising turns out a crowd for an event, while organising builds durable structures and leaders from within. Choose issues that are immediate, specific and winnable.

The method runs listen, identify, build, act, reflect. A good organiser works to become unnecessary and starts on day one. South Asia has its own traditions, from Gandhian constructive work to MKSS and SEWA. Confrontation is not always right: **backlash falls on the people who remain**. Where it is too risky, constructive work, alliances and litigation remain.

key_terms.meaning: The person with power to grant the demand.
A specific, winnable handle on a broad problem.
Turning people out for an event.
A conversation that surfaces real grievances.
Rajasthan group whose hearings led to the social audit.

worked_example.title: Turn problems into issues
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a village meeting names four problems.
steps: No water becomes the Ward 4 handpump, repaired before summer.
Poor schooling becomes the vacant teacher post, filled this term.
Corruption becomes this ration shop, weighing correctly.
Check each: a target who can say yes, a deadline and a visible outcome.
worked_example.answer: Each issue has a target, a clear ask and a deadline. Winning the handpump matters less than what the win teaches.

mistakes: Arriving with the issue, instead of listening for the felt grievance.
Choosing an issue too big to win, which loses the early confidence.
Becoming the leader or spokesperson. Indispensability is a warning sign.

recall.q: What is the difference between mobilising and organising?
recall.a: Mobilising spends power and fades after the event; organising builds structures and leaders that last.

recall.q: What are the five stages?
recall.a: Listen, identify, build, act, reflect.

recall.q: What did Alinsky say about power?
recall.a: It comes from organisation, and it has to be taken because nobody gives it.

recall.q: When does confrontation fit?
recall.a: With a clear duty-bearer, a group large enough to be safe, legal ground and outside allies.

recall.q: Name two South Asian organising traditions.
recall.a: Any two of: Gandhian constructive work, Bhoodan, SEWA, MKSS and the RTI movement, forest and land rights movements.

sections.title: Participatory Tools (PRA / PLA)
sections.big_idea: Participatory tools hand analysis to the community, but **attitudes matter more than techniques**.
in_plain_words: PRA, later PLA, is a family of methods for communities to analyse their own reality, associated with Robert Chambers. The reversal is from extracting data to enabling analysis: the community draws, ranks and analyses on the spot, and the output stays in the village. Core tools are the social map, transect walk, seasonal calendar, wellbeing ranking, Venn diagram and timeline.

Each tool reveals something: the map shows who is left off, the seasonal calendar shows that the lean, borrowing and migration months coincide, and wellbeing ranking shows who is poor by whose definition. PRA can be ritualised, rushed, captured, or raised and betrayed. Chambers' advice: **sit down, shut up, listen**. The hard part is the humility to let go of control.

diagram.caption: what people draw, walk, chart and sort

key_terms.meaning: Participatory Rural Appraisal, later Participatory Learning and Action.
A walk along a line across the village.
A chart of the year's rhythm of work, food and debt.
Households sorted by the community's own criteria.
Chambers' warning against rushed visits.

worked_example.title: Read a seasonal calendar
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a village's calendar shows the lean food month, the heaviest borrowing month and the main migration month all in the same month.
steps: Read the rows together: food stocks, debt and migration.
The lean month, the borrowing month and the migration month are usually the same month.
An annual average hides all three.
So schedule the programme outside the migration month.
worked_example.answer: A training placed in the migration month will not be attended, whatever people say in the meeting.

mistakes: Running a one-day exercise and leaving. It is rushed, and it raises expectations.
Letting the dominant draw the map while the marginalised stay silent.
Publishing household-level wellbeing results. Sorting neighbours in public can expose and offend.

recall.q: Who is PRA associated with?
recall.a: Robert Chambers of IDS, Sussex.

recall.q: What does a social map often reveal through omission?
recall.a: Households left off by the people drawing it, usually the most marginalised.

recall.q: Name two ways PRA fails.
recall.a: Any two of: ritualised, rushed, captured, raised and betrayed.

recall.q: What is the most damaging failure?
recall.a: Raised and betrayed: expectations created and nothing follows.

recall.q: What single sentence prevents most of the harm?
recall.a: Say at the start what can and cannot follow.

sections.title: Self-Help Groups & Collective Action
sections.big_idea: SHGs work through sequence, **save, lend, link, act**, and become community development only at the fourth step.
in_plain_words: An SHG is a small group, usually women, of 10 to 20 members who save regularly into a common fund, lend to one another, link to banks and act on shared concerns. The size limit keeps the mutual knowledge behind peer accountability. SHGs federate into village organisations and cluster or block federations, gaining bargaining power but also the risks of representative bodies.

Commons need collective governance: Ostrom showed the tragedy of the commons can be avoided and listed design principles. DAY-NRLM mobilises women into SHGs at vast scale, building on SERP and Kudumbashree. The caveats are real: over-lending, exclusion of the poorest, paper SHGs, and inclusion without agency. An SHG is **a platform and no cure**.

diagram.caption: federation turns a savings group into a political actor

key_terms.meaning: Small group that saves, lends and acts collectively.
NABARD-led model connecting groups to formal credit.
Upward grouping of SHGs for scale and voice.
Fear that shared resources are inevitably overused.
Penalties that rise with the seriousness of the offence.

worked_example.title: Build a group's fund
worked_example.setup: Illustrative figures: an SHG has 15 members, and each saves Rs 100 a month. The deck gives the size range and the saving-first sequence, and the amounts here are invented.
steps: Size check: 15 is inside the usual 10 to 20 members.
Monthly fund: 15 × 100 = 1,500 rupees.
Yearly fund: 1,500 × 12 = 18,000 rupees.
The group controls this fund and lends from it on its own terms.
worked_example.answer: The group saves Rs 1,500 a month and Rs 18,000 a year. The fund and the habit of meeting are the platform for stage four.

mistakes: Counting groups formed as success. Targets create paper SHGs that never function.
Treating financial inclusion as empowerment. Ask who operates the account.
Assuming a savings group is community development. Many never reach the act stage.

recall.q: What are the four stages of the SHG sequence?
recall.a: Save, lend, link, act.

recall.q: Why is the size limit not incidental?
recall.a: Groups much larger than twenty lose the mutual knowledge that makes peer accountability work.

recall.q: What did Ostrom win and why?
recall.a: The 2009 Nobel Memorial Prize in Economics, for showing communities can sustainably manage common resources.

recall.q: Which landmark models does DAY-NRLM build on?
recall.a: Andhra Pradesh's SERP and Kerala's Kudumbashree.

recall.q: Name two caveats about SHGs.
recall.a: Any two of: over-lending, exclusion of the poorest, paper SHGs, inclusion without agency.

sections.title: Power, Conflict & Elite Capture
sections.big_idea: Ask who decides, who benefits and who is kept out, because ignoring power **hands the outcome to whoever already holds it**.
in_plain_words: Power has three faces: visible (who holds office and signs), hidden (who sets the agenda) and invisible (norms such as this is not for us). Elite capture is when locally powerful people siphon benefits, and participatory programmes are especially exposed. The quiet mechanics are specific: who chairs, when meetings are held, what language is used, who gets the contracts.

Each mechanism has a cheap procedural counter: rotate the chair, let the excluded set the timing, use local language, publish selections. Reading a list aloud is the most effective. Ask of any spokesperson which community, chosen how, accountable to whom. Conflict is normal, and a facilitator is **not neutral about fairness**: protect the weakest party's stake.

children.label: Hidden
items: Shifted by changing who sets it

children.label: Invisible
items: Norms: this is not for us

key_terms.meaning: Who decides, who benefits, who is kept out.
Benefits siphoned by locally powerful people.
Norms that make exclusion feel natural.
Cross-check claims with people not in the room.
Public reading of records.

worked_example.title: Compare attendance with the list
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a village has 120 households on the panchayat list, and 30 attended the meeting that selected beneficiaries.
steps: Households not represented: 120 − 30 = 90.
Share who attended: 30 ÷ 120 = 25%.
Ask who is absent: compare attendance with the household list.
Counter: read the list aloud in a public meeting and hold further rounds.
worked_example.answer: Ninety households were absent, so only 25% had a say. Hold more rounds and read the list aloud.

mistakes: Treating a spokesperson's claim as the community's position. Self-appointed is not elected.
Suppressing conflict to keep a false peace. It preserves the existing imbalance.
Staying neutral between powerful and powerless parties, which sides with the powerful.

recall.q: What are the four power questions in the table?
recall.a: Who decides, who benefits, who is absent, who could block this.

recall.q: Why are participatory programmes more exposed to capture?
recall.a: Decentralisation puts more decisions close to local elites.

recall.q: Name two cheap counters to capture.
recall.a: Any two: rotate the chair, let the excluded set the timing, use local language, publish selection with reasons, read the list aloud.

recall.q: What four questions test a spokesperson?
recall.a: Which community, chosen how, accountable to whom, who disagrees.

recall.q: What are the four steps for handling conflict?
recall.a: Name the interests, separate people from the problem, broaden options, protect the weakest party's stake.

sections.title: Sustainability, Ownership & Exit
sections.big_idea: The measure of the work is what survives, so **plan the exit from day one** and step back deliberately.
in_plain_words: Ask on day one what the community will own, run and fund without you in five years. Dependency is the silent failure: doing what the community could do, convening every meeting and solving every problem teaches people to wait. Ownership comes from who decided, contributed and controlled throughout, so a handover ceremony cannot transfer it.

Watch for four dependency signals and check them at the midpoint. The outsider is a catalyst: guide, connect, coach, and become unnecessary. Withdrawal is graduated through lead, share, support, withdraw, exit, with dates set early. Money after exit comes from member contributions, mainstream finance, earned income and claimed entitlements, and **a new grant is not a plan**.

diagram.caption: a graduated withdrawal with dates set at the start

key_terms.meaning: Relying on an agency for activity, decisions or funds.
The stake that comes from deciding, contributing, controlling.
A fund the institution owns, built during the project.
Gradual, announced and predictable stepping back.
Calling the meetings that the group should call.

worked_example.title: Count your own talking
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: you run a two-hour meeting as the facilitator. The deck says over a quarter of the talking is usually too much.
steps: Meeting length: 2 hours = 120 minutes.
A quarter of 120 minutes: 120 ÷ 4 = 30 minutes.
Count how many minutes you actually speak.
If you spoke more than 30 minutes, step back next time and ask more questions.
worked_example.answer: Thirty minutes is the ceiling. Beyond it you are probably chairing, deciding and supplying the analysis.

mistakes: Writing the exit plan in the final quarter. Every item takes months to arrange.
Reading the absence of dependency signals at the end. Check at the midpoint, when it is correctable.
Staying in the lead role. Phasing without dates collapses into the first phase.

recall.q: What is the day-one question about exit?
recall.a: What will the community own, run and fund without us in five years?

recall.q: Name the five phases of withdrawal.
recall.a: Lead, share, support, withdraw, exit.

recall.q: Name two dependency signals.
recall.a: Any two: nothing happens unless staff convene, problems come to the agency, the committee cannot name its plan, contributions come only from the project.

recall.q: Which exit finance row is most underused?
recall.a: Public funds via the panchayat.

recall.q: What predicts survival two years after exit?
recall.a: The institution still meets and has its own money.

sections.title: Community Development in South Asia
sections.big_idea: Local self-government is the setting, and **the law devolved more than practice delivers**: functions, funds and functionaries.
in_plain_words: Community development plays out through the panchayat in India, the union council in Pakistan, the union parishad in Bangladesh, local levels in Nepal and the pradeshiya sabha in Sri Lanka. India's 73rd Amendment (1992) gave panchayats constitutional status, with three tiers, five-year elections, reservation for SC, ST and women, and a Gram Sabha. States decide the substance.

Reservation has brought more than a million women into office, though proxy leadership persists. DAY-NRLM, watershed development, Joint Forest Management and water user associations are community institutions with recurring weaknesses. The three Fs of devolution are functions, funds and functionaries, and **functionaries usually report to departments**. That gap is where much of the work lives.

key_terms.meaning: 1992 amendment giving panchayati raj constitutional status.
Assembly of all adult voters in a village.
Seats set aside for women, SC and ST.
A husband who exercises his wife's elected office.
Functions, funds and functionaries.

worked_example.title: What reservation delivers
worked_example.setup: Illustrative: a panchayat has 12 elected seats. Reservation for women is one-third in one state and one-half in another, as the deck notes it varies.
steps: With one-third reservation: 12 ÷ 3 = 4 seats for women.
With one-half reservation: 12 ÷ 2 = 6 seats for women.
The quota delivers presence.
Turning presence into authority takes training, protection and a second term.
worked_example.answer: Four or six seats, depending on the state. Presence is not authority, and proxy leadership can follow.

mistakes: Assuming a panchayat can deliver what the statute lists. Check your state's devolution.
Treating the Gram Sabha as a rubber stamp to leave alone. Strengthening it is concrete work.
Copying a landmark model wholesale. Each took a decade or more.

recall.q: What did the 73rd Amendment provide?
recall.a: Three tiers, regular elections, reservation for SC, ST and women, and a Gram Sabha.

recall.q: Which Nepali event devolved substantial powers?
recall.a: The 2015 federal restructuring.

recall.q: What are the three Fs?
recall.a: Functions, funds and functionaries.

recall.q: Which F is the binding constraint?
recall.a: Functionaries, who usually report to departments.

recall.q: Name two landmark models from the table.
recall.a: Any two of: Kudumbashree, SEWA, watershed programmes, AKRSP, Grameen and BRAC.

sections.title: Practice & Pitfalls
sections.big_idea: Guide the group, listen and do no harm, then **measure what is hard to count** and allow the time that trust takes.
in_plain_words: The master skill is facilitation: ask more than you tell, draw out the quiet, make the process visible and be comfortable with silence. Listening has layers, from what is said to what is left unsaid. Apply the do-no-harm lens before you intervene, and remember that stopping suddenly is also an intervention. Five pitfalls recur, each kept alive by an incentive.

Measure the harder signs: groups still meeting after two years, decisions implemented, marginalised members who speak. Realistic timeframes are a year for an SHG, three to five years for a federation, and a decade of support for an institution to survive exit. **A three-year project cannot build a durable institution from nothing**. It can start one, strengthen one, or achieve something else.

right.title: Track
items: Groups still meeting after two years

key_terms.meaning: Helping a group think, decide and act without taking over.
Forming groups to hit a number.
Meetings that change nothing.
Checking side-effects before intervening.
A countable sign of change in people's lives.

worked_example.title: Match the grant to the timeframe
worked_example.setup: The deck says a community institution surviving exit takes about a decade of support, and a federation with bargaining power three to five years. Illustrative: a funder offers a three-year grant.
steps: Years short for institutional survival: 10 − 3 = 7.
Years short for a federation at the upper bound: 5 − 3 = 2.
An SHG takes a year, so it fits the grant.
State plainly what the three years can and cannot achieve.
worked_example.answer: The grant is 7 years short of institutional survival and up to 2 short of a federation. It can start or strengthen a group and should say so.

mistakes: Counting outputs only. The left column shows activity, and the right shows whether it produced anything.
Skipping the do-no-harm question about retaliation. People in visible roles can face costs after you leave.
Promising a durable institution in a three-year project.

recall.q: What are the five pitfalls?
recall.a: Target-chasing, participation theatre, ignoring power, creating dependency, no exit plan.

recall.q: Why does training alone not fix the pitfalls?
recall.a: Each is sustained by an incentive, and ignorance is rarely the cause.

recall.q: Name two things to track instead of counting.
recall.a: Any two, such as groups still meeting after two years or marginalised members who speak.

recall.q: How long does forming a functioning SHG take?
recall.a: About a year of regular meetings.

recall.q: What are the five takeaways' questions?
recall.a: Who decided, who is missing, which rung are we on, what exists here, what runs without us.

notes.2: Use the agenda as a route. Section 1 defines the field, section 2 gives values, section 3 the ladder of participation, sections 4 to 6 the methods, and sections 7 to 9 the institutions, power and exit. Sections 10 and 11 place it in South Asia and in daily practice.
notes.4: Memorise the test of good practice: when the project ends, is the community more able to act on its own future? Every clause in the definition rules something out. Most work called community development fails one clause, usually the second. Service delivery is legitimate; the error is the label.
notes.5: Use the third row as a diagnostic: what is left after exit. A handpump left behind is an output, and a water committee that repairs it is community development. Service delivery measures outputs, and community development measures capacity and voice. Both can be true of one project when the institution is built on purpose.
notes.6: Never say "the community wants" without asking which part and who was in the room. A village is layered by caste, class, gender, religion, age and faction. The cheap corrective is separate group discussions by gender and social group, because mixed groups reliably produce the dominant account.
notes.7: Learn the three senses of community: place, identity, interest. They overlap, so water users cut across caste while the caste groups within do not share water interests. State in your design document which sense you mean. Most confusion in this field comes from sliding between them.
notes.8: Endogenous change comes from within, slower but owned and durable. Exogenous change is faster and well-resourced but can be resented and collapse when funding leaves. Match the mode to the task: a cholera outbreak calls for exogenous action, a village water committee for the endogenous route. Watch for exogenous work reported as endogenous.
notes.9: Follow the four eras: colonial welfare, the 1952 state-led Community Development Programme, the 1970s critique, then participation and rights. The pattern the slide names is that each era's reform became the next era's ritual. Participation is now in that phase, which Section 3 takes up.
notes.10: A beneficiary receives and a citizen claims. The framing changes what a programme builds: a citizen framing needs the entitlement, the office and the route when it fails. It is also more durable, because the programme ends while the entitlement and the panchayat remain.
notes.11: You are a guest: whatever your role, you leave and they stay. The table lists what you carry: resources, status, a timetable and an exit. Courtesy bias follows from status, since people tell visiting agencies what keeps resources coming. That is rational, so read it as information.
notes.13: Learn the five principles and their tests: participation, empowerment, self-determination, equity, sustainability. Each test is behavioural. The third is the hardest and most diagnostic: have you supported a priority you disagreed with? A values statement can be compatible with failing all five.
notes.14: Participation covers everything from being told to deciding, which is why the word alone guarantees nothing. Use the table to name the rung: an awareness camp is informing, a feedback form is consultation, a seat with no vote is placation. State the rung you aim at in the design document, because it can be checked.
notes.15: Empowerment is a process of gaining control, and an agency cannot hand it over. Power is relational, so someone gains only as another's hold weakens, and real work produces friction. If a programme claims empowerment and has produced no friction anywhere, ask what actually changed.
notes.16: Self-determination means the community can set priorities that differ from your logframe. Run the hard test: will you support a decision you disagree with? Check whether a community preference can move your allocation, and say plainly at the start where it cannot. Undisclosed constraints are classic tokenism.
notes.17: A village consensus often reflects who could attend, who could speak and who was heard. A unanimous gram sabha resolution is weak evidence of agreement and strong evidence about who was present. Use separate meetings, secret ballots for sensitive choices and deliberate outreach, and accept that they cost a little more time.
notes.18: Sustainability has five dimensions in the table: social, institutional, financial, ecological and political. The financial row defeats most community institutions, since a group with no independent revenue ends when the grant does. The political row is most neglected, because a link to local government is the route to public resources after you leave.
notes.19: Values show in conduct. Respect is asking before telling, humility is not sitting at the front, transparency is the budget on the wall in the local language, and accountability is a grievance route people use. Displaying the budget publicly is among the cheapest and most consequential things an agency can do.
notes.20: Every principle can be performed without being practised, and the performed version produces the evidence a report requires. Use the two columns as a test: a proposal section against a changed design, an inclusion policy against a meeting held in the Dalit hamlet. A value you cannot check by watching a meeting is not yet operational.
notes.22: Participation is a matter of degree. The right-hand column of the ladder is the whole content: who decides. Use the question "at the end, who signs?" to sort any process. Meetings, forms and committees fit every row, so they prove nothing about power.
notes.23: Learn Arnstein's eight rungs from the bottom: manipulation, therapy, informing, consultation, placation, partnership, delegated power, citizen control. Everything below rung six leaves the decision where it was. The diagram is illustrative, so rely on Arnstein's 1969 paper for the structure.
notes.24: Group the rungs as 1-2 non-participation, 3-5 tokenism, 6-8 citizen power. In tokenism people hear and are heard but lack the power to make their views count. Arnstein's blunt point is that participation without redistribution of power is empty and frustrating for the powerless. The middle band is where the ritual lives.
notes.25: The dangerous rungs are the middle ones because they look participatory. Each tokenism example produces the evidence a donor report asks for, so the monitoring system rewards it. Ask what changed as a result, and not what was produced. If nothing in the design moved, the rung was three or four.
notes.26: Diagnose your own work using the table, since applied to other people it is only a critique. An awareness camp is informing (rung 3), feedback you ignore is consultation (rung 4), a seat with no vote is placation (rung 5). Moving up one rung in a project cycle is realistic. Claiming rung 8 while at rung 4 is more common.
notes.27: Hart's ladder adapts Arnstein's for children, with three false rungs: manipulation, decoration, tokenism. Most of what is photographed at youth events sits there. The upper rungs, up to child-initiated projects with shared decisions, are a far higher bar than most youth engagement is designed to reach.
notes.28: A ladder implies more is always better, but a community may rationally choose to be informed. Ask who chose the level and who opened the space. Cornwall's distinction helps: invited spaces carry different power from claimed ones. What matters is whether the level was chosen or imposed.
notes.30: ABCD flips planning from deficits to assets. Needs assessment gives a list of what is absent and casts the agency as the answer, while asset mapping lists what is present and casts the community as actor. The honest critique, that it can let the state off the hook, is answered by doing both: map assets, then claim entitlements.
notes.31: The deficit lens does quiet harm: the community internalises the framing and learns to wait. Watch for the sign on the first row: asked what they have, people list what they lack. That is a learned response to being surveyed for needs, and it takes deliberate facilitation to move past.
notes.32: Four asset types: individuals, associations, institutions, and physical and natural resources, with the local economy added in the table. The first row carries the sharpest claim: people written off as dependants hold assets. A mapping that omits them repeats the exclusion. A school is an asset that is rarely treated as one.
notes.33: Asset mapping is done together on a shared map, and the act matters because people see their own wealth. Use specific prompts, such as what people here can do well, because a community asked what it has will answer with what it lacks. Leave the map behind, since one the agency keeps is an extraction.
notes.34: Follow the four steps: map, connect, mobilise, add. The breakthrough is often a new connection, such as an SHG linking to the bank, and a new resource is less common. Outside help comes last. Bringing it first makes the agency the source again, whatever the mapping showed.
notes.35: Assets first does not mean self-financed. The serious version of the objection is that self-reliance language can justify withdrawing public provision. The answer is sequence: map what exists, then use the organised community to claim what the state owes. Power analysis is still required, because ABCD can romanticise community.
notes.36: The chart is illustrative and comes from no survey. Its point is the surprise: communities are routinely astonished by how long the skills and gifts column is, because the deficit lens made it invisible. Treat the shape as a facilitation idea to try in your own hamlet.
notes.38: Organising asks how people without power build enough of it to win change from those who have it. Service delivery asks how we deliver. Use the word target: the person with power to grant the demand. Naming them separates a campaign from a complaint. The two traditions mix badly in one team.
notes.39: Alinsky's tradition says change comes from organised people, and power has to be taken because nobody gives it. It is confrontational and American, and it runs alongside indigenous South Asian traditions. Keep the transferable part: name who can grant the demand, and build enough organisation to make refusal costly.
notes.40: A crowd is not an organisation. Mobilising spends power and organising builds it. Use the table: turnout against an organisation, an event against years, external against developed leadership. A big rally with no organisation behind it shows feeling and little power. Do not budget for one and expect the other.
notes.41: Learn the five stages: listen, identify, build, act, reflect. One-to-one conversations are the labour of organising and the part most often cut, and a grievance list from a meeting is different information. Choose issues that are immediate, specific and winnable. Reflection converts a win or a loss into capability.
notes.42: The organiser's test is what continues after they leave, so becoming unnecessary starts on day one. Use the warning signs: being the spokesperson, giving the analysis, chairing every meeting, being indispensable. Indispensability is comfortable, and funders often mistake it for effectiveness.
notes.43: Turn a problem into an issue with a target who can say yes, a deadline and a visible outcome. Poverty becomes wages owed since March, and no water becomes the Ward 4 handpump. Winning small teaches that action works, and that belief is the actual product of early campaigns.
notes.44: South Asia has home-grown organising traditions: Gandhian constructive work, Bhoodan, SEWA, MKSS and the RTI movement, and forest and land rights movements. MKSS's public hearings in Rajasthan in the 1990s are the ancestor of the statutory social audit. Borrow methods critically, because tactics must fit local caste, gender and politics.
notes.45: Confrontation fits when there is a clear duty-bearer, a group large enough to be safe, legal ground and outside allies. It backfires when the target is diffuse or the marginalised are few and exposed. Backlash falls on those who remain, so the decision belongs to them. Alternatives include constructive work and litigation.
notes.47: PRA is a family of methods for communities to analyse their own reality, associated with Robert Chambers. Remember the literal meaning of handing over the stick: the person drawing the map on the ground is doing the analysis. The methods spread fast in the 1990s and were often reduced to a toolkit.
notes.48: Compare extraction with enabling. In a conventional survey the outsider analyses elsewhere, and in PRA the community analyses on the spot, so the village holds the output. The immediacy is the underrated advantage. The risks differ and neither is smaller: a badly run PRA extracts data and also raises expectations.
notes.49: Learn the six tools and the question each answers: social map, transect walk, seasonal calendar, wellbeing ranking, Venn diagram, timeline. The map's value is often in who is omitted. Check it against a list such as the ration shop's, and omissions become a finding.
notes.50: Mapping works without literacy, in public, quickly, and the output stays in the village. The analytical strength is correctability: a map drawn in public is argued over, and the argument is more informative than the map. Photograph it and leave a copy behind for later negotiations with the panchayat.
notes.51: A seasonal calendar shows the rhythm of vulnerability that an annual average hides. Read the rows together: the lean month, the borrowing month and the migration month are usually the same month. Use it to schedule programmes, since an activity planned for the migration month will not be attended.
notes.52: Wellbeing ranking lets the community sort its own households by its own criteria, and it regularly produces a different poorest group than a survey line. That difference is a finding. It is sensitive, so run it with a small group, discreetly, and never publish household-level results.
notes.53: Four ways PRA fails: ritualised, rushed, captured, and raised and betrayed. The last is most damaging, because a community that has analysed its problems expects action and repeated disappointment ends cooperation. Say at the start what can and cannot follow. Chambers himself warned of PRA tourism.
notes.54: Behaviour matters more than technique. Learn the four behaviours and what each prevents: sit down, shut up and listen; be patient; hand over the stick; embrace error. The methods spread faster than the behaviours, so much labelled PRA is a facilitator drawing while the community watches. Learn to wait.
notes.56: An SHG is a small group, usually women-only with 10 to 20 members, that saves regularly, lends internally and links to banks. The size limit is deliberate, because larger groups lose the mutual knowledge behind peer accountability. Saving before borrowing builds a fund the group controls.
notes.57: Learn the sequence: save, lend, link, act. The fourth stage makes an SHG community development and moves it beyond finance, and many groups never reach it. A group that only saves and lends is a savings group. SHG-Bank Linkage, developed through NABARD from the early 1990s, made the model scalable.
notes.58: SHGs federate into village organisations and then cluster or block federations. Federation turns a savings group into a political actor that can hold a line department to account. It also brings the risks of any representative structure: distance from members, capture of office, and speaking for groups that did not decide.
notes.59: Commons such as grazing land, forests, fisheries and groundwater are what poor communities depend on, and the heaviest dependants are the least powerful. Ostrom showed the tragedy of the commons is avoidable. Groundwater is the hardest case in South Asia because its boundary is invisible.
notes.60: Ostrom's design principles become practical questions: who is a member, were the rules made here, can users change them, who monitors, is the first offence treated as the fifth, is conflict resolution fast and cheap? Graduated sanctions are most often missing in designed institutions, which tend toward no enforcement or one severe penalty.
notes.61: DAY-NRLM mobilises rural poor women into SHGs and federations at vast scale, building on Andhra Pradesh's SERP and Kerala's Kudumbashree. The slide pairs each feature with a risk: targets against quality, representation questions, over-lending. Mobilisation targets pressure groups to form quickly, and quickly-formed groups are the ones that do not function.
notes.62: The chart is illustrative: read the shape, which is sustained rapid growth into the millions, and do not quote exact figures. Scale brings bargaining power and policy attention, and also pressure to hit formation targets. At this scale the average tells you little. What matters is whether a particular group functions.
notes.63: SHGs are a platform and no cure. Learn the four caveats and the check for each: over-lending (multiple borrowing), exclusion of the poorest, paper SHGs (minutes and savings continuity), and inclusion without agency. Ask who operates the account, because financial inclusion figures count accounts and say nothing about who decides.
notes.65: Power is always in the room. Ask who decides, who benefits, who is kept out and who could block it. Watch who speaks last, trace the last three contracts, compare attendance with the household list. Ignoring power hands the outcome to whoever already had it, with the legitimacy of a participatory process.
notes.66: Learn three faces of power: visible (who holds office), hidden (who sets the agenda) and invisible (norms such as "this is not for us"). The framing comes from Lukes. The third is slowest to shift and keeps most exclusion in place. An open invitation does not reach a woman who considers the meeting not hers.
notes.67: Elite capture is when locally powerful people siphon a programme's benefits. Participatory programmes are more exposed, because handing power to the community can hand it to whoever dominates it. The counters are procedural: multiple rounds, lists read aloud, rotation, published criteria. None needs anyone to become less powerful.
notes.68: Capture looks like the natural order: the dominant chair "because they have time", meetings at times the poor cannot attend, jargon, contracts to the same families. Each counter is cheap and procedural. Reading a beneficiary list aloud in public is the most effective, and it is the basis of the social audit.
notes.69: The marginalised village is itself stratified. For each excluded group the table names a mechanism: women (timing, mobility, permission), Dalits (seating, location), Adivasis (distance, language), persons with disabilities (access), the landless. Mechanisms are specific, so fixes differ. Hold the meeting in the Dalit hamlet.
notes.70: When someone says the community wants this, ask four questions: which community, chosen how, accountable to whom, who disagrees. Unanimity is a warning. Triangulate with people who were not in the room. The questions are fair to everyone, and they protect real representatives as much as they expose false ones.
notes.71: Conflict is normal and useful: it can mean long-suppressed interests are being voiced. Suppressing it preserves the imbalance. A process with no disagreement anywhere has probably not touched anything that matters. The facilitator's job is to keep conflict safe, in the open and focused on interests.
notes.72: Four steps for conflict: name the interests, separate people from the problem, broaden options, protect the weakest party's stake. The last is where neutrality ends, because a facilitator who stays neutral between powerful and powerless takes the powerful side. Say so at the start: that is a rule, and no bias.
notes.74: Plan the exit from day one and build backwards from the five-year question: what will the community own, run and fund without us? Every item in the table takes months to arrange, so none fits the final quarter. Write the exit plan into the proposal.
notes.75: Dependency is created by doing what the community could do, convening every meeting and solving every problem. The right column matters: giving resources and being present do not create it. The commonest route is the sympathetic one, solving a problem quickly because the community would take longer and might fail.
notes.76: Ownership comes from who decided, contributed and controlled throughout, and a handover ceremony cannot transfer it. Use the table: deciding, contributing, controlling resources, selecting leaders. Contribution need not be cash, since labour, land, time and materials create a stake, and a small contribution from the start works better.
notes.77: Check four dependency signals: nothing happens unless staff convene, problems go to the agency, the committee cannot name its plan, contributions come only from the project. Let one meeting fail. Do the check at the midpoint and not the end, because all four are correctable while the programme runs.
notes.78: The outsider is a catalyst and facilitator, a role apart from provider or chief. Use the Do and Do not columns: coach leaders, ask questions, become unnecessary. The role is hard because the right-hand column is faster and rewarded by reporting systems. Count your share of the talking; over a quarter is usually too much.
notes.79: Phase out in five steps: lead, share, support, withdraw, exit. The table shows who convenes and who decides at each. Set dates for each transition at the start and announce the exit date early, because phasing without dates collapses into the first phase. Communities plan differently when they know.
notes.80: The chart is illustrative and comes from no study, but it names a real pattern: what a community builds it keeps. Two years after exit, ask whether the institution still meets and has its own money. Follow-up that long after closure is cheap, rarely done, and the only real measure of this work.
notes.81: Financial sustainability is the hardest kind, so plan where money comes from after exit: member contributions, linkage to mainstream finance, earned income, claimed entitlements. A corpus built from year one is substantial by closure. A new grant is no plan. The panchayat route is the most underused.
notes.83: Community development plays out through local self-government: the panchayat in India, the union council in Pakistan, the union parishad in Bangladesh, local levels in Nepal, the pradeshiya sabha in Sri Lanka. Know which body holds which function, because it decides whom your community organisation negotiates with. Nepal's 2015 restructuring devolved unusually substantial powers.
notes.84: The 73rd Amendment (1992) gave panchayats constitutional status with three tiers, five-year elections, reservation for SC, ST and women, and a gram sabha. It left substance to states, so power varies between Kerala and most of north India. Check your state's devolution before advising what the panchayat can deliver.
notes.85: The Gram Sabha is the assembly of all adult voters and the only face-to-face democratic body in the system. On paper it approves plans, selects beneficiaries and holds the panchayat to account. In practice it often ratifies. Strengthen it with advance notice, timing for women and workers, a circulated agenda, minutes read aloud and quorum.
notes.86: Reservation brought more than a million women and lakhs of Dalit and Adivasi citizens into office, and who holds the seat changes what gets built. Proxy leadership, the sarpanch-pati, persists. Both are true. A quota delivers presence, and converting presence into authority takes training, protection and a second term.
notes.87: DAY-NRLM threads community development through the state: SHGs and federations link to banks, run social-audit processes and increasingly interface with the panchayat. The key word is convergence: federations, MGNREGA, the panchayat and line departments woven together at the village so the pieces reinforce each other.
notes.88: Watershed development, Joint Forest Management and water user associations are textbook commons: they succeed where users make and enforce their own rules. Each has a recurring weakness in the table, and benefit follows existing land and power unless the design counters it. Watershed work raises land values, so design explicitly for the landless.
notes.89: Study the models critically: Kudumbashree, SEWA, watershed programmes, AKRSP, Grameen and BRAC. Take the transferable lesson, such as organising by occupation or public reading of records, and leave the template. The common feature is a durable institution, and each took a decade or more.
notes.90: Learn the three Fs: functions, funds, functionaries. The law devolved all three, but functionaries usually report to departments, which is the binding constraint. A panchayat that cannot direct the staff in its area cannot deliver. Much practitioner work is helping communities claim powers the law already grants.
notes.92: Facilitation helps a group think, decide and act without taking over: the facilitator owns the process and the community owns the content. Practise the moves in the table: ask, wait through the silence, invite the quiet, summarise what was said, let the group decide. The second and third answers are the useful ones.
notes.93: Listening is a technique with five layers: what is said, who says it, who does not speak, what is left unsaid and what is said afterwards. The conversation on the walk back is often more accurate than the meeting. Keep a two-minute record of who spoke and who did not.
notes.94: Intervention is never neutral, so ask before acting: who gains status, who loses, could this deepen a division, could someone face retaliation, what if we stop suddenly? The fourth carries real consequences, since visible participants can face costs after you leave. Ending a programme abruptly redistributes power.
notes.95: Learn the five pitfalls with their antidotes: target-chasing, participation theatre, ignoring power, creating dependency, no exit plan. Each persists because of an incentive, so training alone does not fix them. Change what is reported and most move. A report asking who is not in the group changes field behaviour.
notes.96: Replace counting with tracking: groups formed with groups still meeting after two years, meetings held with decisions implemented, members enrolled with marginalised members who speak. Every measure on the right is countable but smaller and slower. Report both columns, and combine numbers with stories.
notes.97: Trust, organisation and leadership grow at the speed of relationships. Learn the realistic timeframes: a functioning SHG takes a year, a federation with bargaining power three to five years, and a community institution surviving exit a decade of support. A three-year project can start something, strengthen it, or achieve something else and say so.
notes.98: Use the reading list by purpose: Chambers for participatory practice, Ostrom for the commons, Kretzmann and McKnight for ABCD, Alinsky for organising. The slide calls it short and honest. Pair it with ImpactMojo's Qualitative Methods, Gender Mainstreaming and Political Economy 101 courses.
notes.99: Turn each takeaway into a question you can ask in any meeting: who decided, who is missing, which rung are we on, what exists here, what runs without us. If you keep one, keep the second, because almost every failure begins with treating a village as a single voice.
